title: Content-Security-Policy img-src allows a wildcard source
description: The Content-Security-Policy img-src directive allows a bare wildcard source: the token `*` or a scheme wildcard such as `https://*` appears inside that directive's source list. The policy therefore permits the browser to load the affected resource type from any origin, which is the opposite of what a restrictive policy is meant to express. Images can be loaded from any origin, so injected markup or a third-party script can beacon page-derived data out in image requests that need no script execution and no cors grant.
remediation: Replace the wildcard in img-src with the explicit origins that must be reachable, and use 'none' or 'self' where no third-party origin is needed. If the wildcard was added to unblock a single vendor, name that vendor's origin instead so the policy keeps recording intent.
limitation: One header value and one directive. The rule judges img-src only when it is written in the policy; when the directive is absent, the default-src or child-src fallback decides the behaviour and other rules report that case. Values are matched lexically, so an origin wildcard such as *.example.com is not treated as a bare wildcard.
scopeT: One response whose Content-Security-Policy carries an explicit img-src directive whose source list contains `*` or a scheme wildcard.
fp: A policy that deliberately allows a wide CDN pool can still be flagged; the finding is the wildcard, not proof that a third-party origin is reachable in the deployment.
recordDesc: The Content-Security-Policy img-src directive contains a bare wildcard, so image subresources may come from any origin. Image requests are the cheapest exfiltration channel available to injected markup: a crafted URL carries the data in the path and the browser sends it without a script execution or a CORS preflight.
applicability: HTTPS responses that send Content-Security-Policy with an explicit img-src directive.
risk: Page data can leave through image requests to attacker-chosen hosts; MEDIUM severity because the channel needs an injection point to start from.
why: The img-src directive contains the token `*` or a scheme wildcard rather than an explicit origin list.
fix: List the concrete origins in img-src.
Re-fetch the endpoint and confirm the directive no longer contains `*`.
verifyT: Request the endpoint and read the img-src directive; the wildcard token must be gone and the remaining origins must be ones you operate or trust.

cells.name: img-src allows a wildcard source
cells.safe: policy lists explicit origins

title: Content-Security-Policy strict-dynamic without a nonce or hash
description: The Content-Security-Policy script-src directive lists 'strict-dynamic' but carries no nonce or hash source. A browser that implements strict-dynamic ignores host and scheme sources in that directive only when a nonce or hash is present to bootstrap the trust chain; without one the keyword does not establish the delegation the policy author expected.
remediation: Add a per-response nonce (or a hash of the allowed inline script) to script-src alongside 'strict-dynamic', and template the nonce into the script tags the page emits. Keep the host allowlist only for browsers that do not support strict-dynamic.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the keyword combination the policy states; it does not test browser behaviour and cannot see whether the application intended a nonce that failed to render.
scopeT: One response whose Content-Security-Policy script-src directive contains 'strict-dynamic' and no nonce or hash source.
fp: A policy staged for a browser-support rollout may carry strict-dynamic before the nonce wiring lands; the combination is still the reportable fact.
recordDesc: The Content-Security-Policy script-src directive uses 'strict-dynamic' without a nonce or hash. In browsers that support the keyword, the delegation model starts from a trusted nonce or hash, so a policy without one keeps falling back to the host allowlist the author meant to retire.
applicability: HTTPS responses that send Content-Security-Policy with a script-src directive.
risk: The policy gives the appearance of strict script delegation without the bootstrap it needs; LOW severity because host sources still apply.
why: script-src contains 'strict-dynamic' and no 'nonce-, 'sha256-, 'sha384- or 'sha512- source.
fix: Add a per-response nonce to script-src.
Template the nonce into every script tag the page emits.
verifyT: Fetch the response twice: script-src must list 'strict-dynamic' together with a fresh 'nonce- value each time.

cells.safe: strict-dynamic is paired with a fresh nonce

title: Content-Security-Policy sandbox grants both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin
description: The Content-Security-Policy sandbox directive lists both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin. Together they let sandboxed content run script and keep the origin of the embedding document, which is the documented way to remove the sandbox's protection: the framed document can reach the same-origin DOM and storage it was supposed to be isolated from.
remediation: Drop one of the two tokens. A frame that must run script should not keep its origin (allow-scripts alone), and a frame that must keep its origin should not run script. Serve untrusted content from a separate origin instead of weakening the sandbox.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the token combination in the sandbox directive; it cannot tell which content the policy applies to or whether the frame is same-origin in practice.
scopeT: One response whose Content-Security-Policy sandbox directive contains both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin.
fp: A sandbox that deliberately frames same-origin application code is reported; the token pair still removes the isolation the directive exists to give.
recordDesc: The Content-Security-Policy sandbox directive grants allow-scripts and allow-same-origin at the same time. Content framed under that policy keeps the embedding origin, so script inside the frame can reach the parent document's DOM, cookies and storage, and the sandbox stops being a boundary.
applicability: HTTPS responses that send Content-Security-Policy with a sandbox directive.
risk: The sandbox no longer isolates framed content from the embedding origin; MEDIUM severity because the frame escapes the intended boundary.
why: The sandbox directive lists both allow-scripts and allow-same-origin.
fix: Remove allow-same-origin from sandboxed frames that run script.
Serve untrusted content from a separate origin.
verifyT: Fetch the response and confirm the sandbox directive no longer lists both tokens together.

cells.name: sandbox grants allow-scripts and allow-same-origin
cells.safe: sandbox keeps at most one of the two tokens

title: Content-Security-Policy carries an obsolete or removed directive
description: The Content-Security-Policy value contains a directive that browsers no longer implement (plugin-types, reflected-xss, referrer or disown-opener). The directive looks like a control in review, but no browser acts on it, so the policy records an intent that is not enforced.
remediation: Remove the obsolete directive and express the same intent with a control that is still implemented: frame-ancestors or the Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header instead of disown-opener, Referrer-Policy instead of the referrer directive, and object-src 'none' instead of plugin-types.
limitation: One header value. The rule matches the directive names that are documented as removed or non-implemented; it does not evaluate whether the policy still achieves the intended control through another directive.
scopeT: One response whose Content-Security-Policy contains a removed directive name.
fp: Policies generated by older frameworks often carry these tokens; the finding is that the control is inert, not that the site is unprotected overall.
recordDesc: The Content-Security-Policy contains a directive that current browsers do not implement. Reviewers reading the policy count the directive as a control, while the browser ignores it, so the policy overstates what it enforces and the replacement control may never have been configured.
applicability: HTTPS responses that send Content-Security-Policy.
risk: The policy appears to enforce a control that no browser applies; LOW severity because the missing protection is a gap, not an active weakness.
why: The policy lists plugin-types, reflected-xss, referrer or disown-opener.
fix: Remove the removed directive.
Express the intent with frame-ancestors, Referrer-Policy or object-src instead.
verifyT: Fetch the response and confirm the policy no longer lists the removed directive, and that the replacement control is present.

cells.name: obsolete directive present
cells.safe: policy uses only implemented directives

title: Strict-Transport-Security delivered over plaintext HTTP
description: The response carrying Strict-Transport-Security was fetched over http://. User agents ignore the header on a non-secure response, so the policy is not installed even though every configuration review sees an HSTS header. The site keeps its first-visit downgrade window while appearing to have closed it.
remediation: Serve HSTS only from the HTTPS listener, and make the HTTP listener answer with a redirect to HTTPS that does not pretend to set the policy. Check the proxy configuration for an add_header rule that is applied to both listeners.
limitation: One response and its scheme. The rule judges the secured-ness of the response that carried the header; it cannot see whether the HTTPS listener sets the header correctly.
scopeT: One response fetched over http:// that carries a non-empty Strict-Transport-Security header.
fp: A test listener that mirrors production headers over plaintext is reported; browsers ignore the header there, which is the finding.
recordDesc: The Strict-Transport-Security header arrived on a response fetched over plaintext HTTP. Browsers only accept HSTS from a secure transport, so the policy is discarded, the connection stays downgradable, and the presence of the header gives reviewers a false assurance that the policy is installed.
applicability: Responses fetched over http:// that carry Strict-Transport-Security.
risk: HSTS is never installed despite the header being present; MEDIUM severity because the downgrade path stays open on every plaintext visit.
why: The observation URL scheme is http: and the response carries a non-empty Strict-Transport-Security header.
fix: Remove the header from the HTTP listener.
Set it on the HTTPS listener only, behind a permanent redirect.
verifyT: Request the http:// endpoint and confirm no Strict-Transport-Security header is returned, then request https:// and confirm the header is present.

cells.name: HSTS sent over plaintext HTTP
cells.safe: HSTS is served only over HTTPS

title: Set-Cookie carries an unrecognised SameSite value
description: A Set-Cookie header names SameSite with a value that is not Strict, Lax or None, or names the attribute with no value at all. A user agent cannot interpret the attribute, so it falls back to its own default policy: the site does not get the cross-site behaviour it declared, and the cookie may be sent on cross-site requests the author meant to block.
remediation: Send one of the three defined values, spelled exactly: SameSite=Strict, SameSite=Lax or SameSite=None together with Secure. Fix the template or framework setting that produced the misspelling so the attribute cannot regress.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the attribute token as written and never infers the browser's fallback for a particular version; a cookie the browser discards is also reported, because the header is still wrong.
scopeT: One response whose Set-Cookie header names SameSite with an undefined value or with no value.
fp: A value from a newer specification revision than the scanner knows would be reported; the three values above are the ones browsers implement.
recordDesc: A Set-Cookie header carries a SameSite attribute whose value is not one of Strict, Lax or None, or carries the attribute without a value. Browsers discard an uninterpretable value and apply their default cross-site policy, so the cookie's cross-site behaviour is not the one the response declares.
applicability: Responses that set cookies.
risk: The cookie is sent under the browser default policy rather than the declared one; LOW severity because the outcome depends on the browser default.
why: The SameSite attribute value is not strict, lax or none (case-insensitive), or the attribute has no value.
fix: Correct the SameSite value to Strict, Lax or None.
Add Secure whenever SameSite=None is used.
verifyT: Fetch the response and confirm every SameSite attribute carries one of the three defined values.

cells.name: SameSite value is not recognised
cells.safe: SameSite is Strict, Lax or None

title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin uses a wildcard inside an origin
description: The Access-Control-Allow-Origin value is a scheme plus a host pattern that contains a wildcard character. CORS does not define wildcard hosts: the value must be either the literal * or one exact origin, so a browser matches this header against no origin and the credentialed request the developer intended to permit fails. A proxy or framework that rewrites origins may also be reflecting attacker input into this header.
remediation: Return one exact origin, echoed from a server-side allowlist after comparing the request's Origin header, or return the literal * when the response is not credentialed. Remove host-pattern support from the CORS helper that produced the value.
limitation: One header value. The rule judges the declared origin pattern; it cannot see the request's Origin header and therefore cannot tell whether the value was reflected from attacker input.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Allow-Origin value contains a wildcard inside a scheme-and-host form.
fp: A deployment that relies on a proxy expanding the pattern is reported; the header as observed is not a valid CORS origin.
recordDesc: Access-Control-Allow-Origin carries a scheme and host pattern with a wildcard character in it. The CORS protocol only permits the literal * or one exact origin, so the browser matches nothing, credentialed cross-origin reads fail, and the policy records an origin-sharing intent it does not implement.
applicability: Responses that send Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
risk: The CORS policy silently fails or reflects too widely, depending on how the value is generated; LOW severity because the common outcome is a broken grant.
why: The value starts with http:// or https:// and contains * before the path separator.
fix: Echo one exact origin from a server-side allowlist.
Use the literal * only for non-credentialed responses.
verifyT: Send a request with an Origin header and confirm Access-Control-Allow-Origin returns exactly that origin or the literal *.

cells.name: origin pattern contains a wildcard
cells.safe: a single exact origin is returned

title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is not a bare origin
description: The Access-Control-Allow-Origin value carries a path or a trailing slash after the host. An origin, by definition, has no path component, so a browser never matches this value; the cross-origin read the configuration intended to allow is blocked, and the misconfiguration usually points at a CORS helper that concatenates configuration strings instead of parsing origins.
remediation: Compare the request Origin against an allowlist and echo the origin exactly, with no path, no trailing slash and no query. Fix the helper so configuration values are parsed as URLs and reduced to scheme, host and port.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the shape of the declared origin and cannot observe whether the browser rejected the response.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Allow-Origin value has a path component or trailing slash.
fp: A policy file kept in source control that is not served on the wire is out of scope; the finding is the header the browser receives.
recordDesc: Access-Control-Allow-Origin contains a path or a trailing slash after the host. A browser compares the value against the requesting origin, which never carries a path, so the match fails and the response is denied to the site the operator meant to trust.
applicability: Responses that send Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
risk: Cross-origin access is denied for the intended site while the configuration looks correct; LOW severity because it is a functional break, not an exposure.
why: The value begins with a scheme and host followed by a path separator.
fix: Echo the origin with no path component.
Parse configured origins as URLs before echoing them.
verifyT: Send a request with an Origin header and confirm the response value equals the origin exactly, with no trailing slash.

cells.name: origin carries a path
cells.safe: a bare origin is returned

title: Referrer-Policy names no policy a browser recognises
description: The Referrer-Policy header is present but none of its comma-separated tokens is a policy a browser implements. Browsers skip unknown tokens, so with no recognised token left the header has no effect and the default policy applies: full URLs are sent to same-scheme destinations, which leaks paths and query strings that the header was meant to trim.
remediation: Use one of the defined policy tokens, spelled exactly (no-referrer, same-origin, strict-origin-when-cross-origin and the other five). Add a test that fails when the configured value is not in the allowed list, because a misspelled token fails silently in the browser.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports that no token is recognised; it does not evaluate which default the deployed browser then applies, and a header with at least one recognised token is left to the value rules.
scopeT: One response whose Referrer-Policy header contains tokens but none of them is a defined policy.
fp: A future policy token would be reported until the rule list is updated; the eight tokens above are the ones the specification defines.
recordDesc: The Referrer-Policy header carries only tokens that are not defined policies. Browsers ignore unknown tokens and fall back to the default policy, so the site sends full referrer URLs to same-scheme destinations while its configuration reads as if referrer trimming were enabled.
applicability: Responses that send Referrer-Policy.
risk: Referrer URLs leak despite an explicit policy header; LOW severity because the leak is confined to same-scheme destinations.
why: No comma-separated token in the header is one of the eight defined Referrer-Policy values.
fix: Correct the token to a defined policy.
Add a configuration test that rejects unknown tokens.
verifyT: Fetch the response and confirm the header value is one of the eight defined tokens.

cells.name: no recognised Referrer-Policy token
cells.safe: the header names a defined policy

title: Refresh header targets a script scheme
description: The Refresh header carries a url= target whose scheme is javascript: or vbscript:. The header exists to send the browser to another document, so a script scheme turns a redirect control into an inline script sink: wherever the value is derived from request data, an attacker can place markup that executes in the page origin.
remediation: Build the Refresh target from a fixed allowlist of paths, not from request data, and never emit a script scheme. Prefer an HTTP 3xx redirect, which cannot carry a script scheme, and treat any existing javascript: target in configuration as a defect to remove.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the scheme the header names; it cannot prove the value is attacker-influenced, and some browsers block Refresh navigation to script schemes outright, so impact depends on the client.
scopeT: One response whose Refresh header names a javascript: or vbscript: URL.
fp: A static page that deliberately uses a script-scheme refresh is reported; the construct is unsafe wherever the value can change.
recordDesc: The Refresh header points at a javascript: or vbscript: URL. Meta-refresh navigation is normally a redirect control, but a script scheme makes it execute code in the current origin, so a value that reaches this header from request data becomes a script-injection sink.
applicability: Responses that send a Refresh header.
risk: A redirect control is turned into script execution in the page origin; MEDIUM severity because impact depends on whether the target is attacker-influenced.
why: The Refresh value names url=javascript: or url=vbscript:.
fix: Remove the script-scheme target.
Replace the refresh with an HTTP 3xx redirect to an allowlisted path.
verifyT: Fetch the response and confirm the Refresh target is a path or an https URL you operate, never a script scheme.

cells.name: Refresh targets a script scheme
cells.safe: Refresh targets an allowlisted path

title: X-DNS-Prefetch-Control explicitly enables DNS prefetching
description: The response sets X-DNS-Prefetch-Control to on. That value tells the browser it may resolve hostnames for links before the user follows them, which turns page content into outbound DNS queries. On pages that render user-supplied links or private hostnames this discloses browsing intent and can confirm which records a visitor viewed.
remediation: Send X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off on authenticated and administrative pages, or omit the header and rely on the browser default for the pages where prefetching is useful.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the explicit enablement; it cannot see whether the page actually contains links to hosts worth prefetching.
scopeT: One response whose X-DNS-Prefetch-Control value is on.
fp: A public marketing site that wants prefetching for speed is reported; the value is still an explicit choice to resolve hostnames early.
recordDesc: The response sets X-DNS-Prefetch-Control to on, so the browser may resolve hostnames found in page links before a visitor follows them. Content that renders user-supplied links therefore produces outbound DNS lookups that reveal which hosts a visitor was shown.
applicability: Responses that send X-DNS-Prefetch-Control.
risk: Rendered links produce outbound DNS traffic that discloses browsing intent; LOW severity because the disclosure is limited to hostname resolution.
why: The X-DNS-Prefetch-Control value is on (case-insensitive).
fix: Send X-DNS-Prefetch-Control: off on sensitive pages.

title: Origin-Agent-Cluster explicitly disables origin-keyed agent clustering
description: The response sets Origin-Agent-Cluster to ?0, which opts the document out of origin-keyed agent clustering. recordDesc: The response sets Origin-Agent-Cluster to ?0, opting out of origin-keyed agent clustering. Same-site documents that would otherwise be isolated then share an agent cluster, so a weaker same-site origin runs alongside the application rather than in its own process boundary.
applicability: Responses that send Origin-Agent-Cluster.
risk: Same-site documents share an agent cluster with the application; LOW severity because the isolation loss only matters once another same-site origin is compromised.
why: The Origin-Agent-Cluster value is ?0.
fix: Send Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1.
Remove the opt-out unless a documented dependency requires it.

title: Environment file contents disclosed in a response
description: The response body carries environment-file assignments: an APP_KEY entry together with an APP_ENV entry. That pair identifies a framework .env file, which holds the application key, database credentials and third-party tokens in plain text.
remediation: Stop serving dotfiles from the document root, move the environment file outside it, and rotate every secret it contained.
limitation: Two body markers. A documentation page that shows a redacted .env example is reported only if both assignments appear unredacted in the body.
scopeT: One response whose body contains APP_KEY and APP_ENV assignments.
fp: A deployment that intentionally publishes a redacted sample is reported if the two assignments are present; the rule cannot judge redaction.
recordDesc: The response served a framework environment file containing the APP_KEY and APP_ENV entries. That file holds the key that signs cookies and encrypted values plus the database and mail credentials, so reading it is equivalent to reading the deployment secrets.
applicability: Responses that return a dotenv file from the document root.
risk: Application secrets are readable in plain text; HIGH severity because the key material is directly usable.
why: The body contains APP_KEY= and APP_ENV= assignments.
fix: Block dotfiles at the web server.
Move the environment file above the document root and rotate the secrets.
verifyT: Request the environment file path and confirm the server returns 404 or 403, and that no assignment lines are returned.
